title: Nagasena's chariot
hookLine: conventional truth (people, tables) and ultimate truth (momentary mind and matter)
carry: two truths, both true: the chariot and its parts

lines: GRAB THE CHAIR BY THE WINDOW.
cards: Someone in the kitchen asks you to grab the chair by the window. Nobody answers: which collection of wooden parts, held together by glue and screws, do you mean? And yet the second answer isn't wrong.
Two days ago there was a puzzle on the shelf: a book that takes people apart into moments, right next to a book that sorts kinds of people. Today, the key: two ways of speaking, both of them true.

teach.b: The commentaries name them. Conventional truth is the way the world talks: people, tables, chairs, a mother, a son.

Ultimate truth is the way the Abhidhamma talks: moments of mind and bits of matter, arising and passing away. First, the old picture. In the Questions of King Milinda, a monk named Nagasena asks the king how he came.
By chariot. Is the pole the chariot? No.
The wheels, the axle, the frame, the seat? No, no, no. Is there a chariot apart from all those?
So where is the chariot? The king works it out: chariot is a name used for all those parts put together. And Nagasena says his own name works the same way.

In a discourse in the Digha Nikaya, after a long talk about the self, he says, in paraphrase, that words like these are the world's ordinary expressions, and he uses them without being misled by them.
He said I and you, and told stories about kings and farmers. Third, the point that makes the puzzle go away.
It means agreed on, useful, how a life gets lived. You can't keep a promise to a stream of mind-moments; you keep it to your sister. That's why the book of persons belongs in the basket.
Fourth, why the second way matters. Speaking only the first way, it's easy to think there's a solid someone in there, the same yesterday and tomorrow.
The second way lets a person see the parts, so anger or pride is seen as weather passing through, not as who they are.

how: Theravada teachers use the two truths, conventional and ultimate, to explain how the Buddha could speak of persons while teaching not-self, and the chariot of Nagasena is a common teaching story.

games.q: what does “two ways of speaking” mean?
o: speaking to monks one way and to lay people another
talking of chairs and people, or of moments and matter
a polite way and a blunt way to say the same thing

games.q: two ways of speaking: tap the pairs.
p: a name for the parts put together

s: in the Abhidhamma, conventional truth means lies
conventional means agreed on and useful: how a life gets lived. you keep a promise to your sister, not to mind-moments.
the Buddha used words like I and you
in the Digha Nikaya he calls them the world's ordinary expressions, used without being misled by them.
Nagasena finds the chariot in its wheels
not the pole, the wheels, the axle or the seat: chariot is a name for all of them together.

games.q: you're King Milinda. the monk asks: is the pole the chariot? the wheels? the axle? is there a chariot apart from them? what do you conclude?
o: there is no chariot and I walked here
chariot is a name for the parts put together
the chariot is really the seat
games.why: the king works it out: chariot is a name used for all those parts together, and Nagasena says his own name works the same way.

practice: If you'd like, choose one thing near you, a cup, say, and describe it the ordinary way: my cup, the blue one, a gift. Then slowly the other way: a shape seen, a color, a hardness, a thought that says mine.
Then turn it on yourself, me, sitting here, and then breath moving, a pressure where the body meets the seat, sounds arriving, and let both be true.

wordCard.voice: Two ways of speaking. Conventional truth, people and tables, and ultimate truth, moments of mind and matter, each true in its own way. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: convention, what is agreed on; sammuti-sacca is conventional truth.

carryVoice: Your line: two truths, both true, the chariot and its parts. Conventional doesn't mean false. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 9 (Potthapada Sutta), closing passage on the world's expressions
Commentarial teaching on the two truths (sammuti-sacca and paramattha-sacca), e.g. Kathavatthu commentary
